analysis.one_liner: Lets the government fine companies up to 15-30% of US revenue for illegal monopoly conduct.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let antitrust enforcers impose large fines on monopolistic companies, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission can go to court to stop companies from illegally maintaining monopolies, but they cannot impose fines just for that conduct—the usual result is a court order and, in private suits, damages paid to customers. This bill would have let DOJ and the FTC seek civil penalties of up to 15% of a company's total US revenue, or 30% of the revenue in the market where the illegal conduct occurred, on top of existing remedies. The two agencies would also have had to write joint guidelines explaining how they would size the penalties. The bill was never taken up by the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses that compete against dominant firms. By adding a real financial penalty to the tools available against illegal monopoly conduct, the bill aimed to deter companies from using their market power to lock out competitors, keep prices high, or degrade quality.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and small businesses facing dominant firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let DOJ and the FTC recover civil penalties from companies that violate the Sherman Act's ban on monopolistic conduct, such as exclusionary practices like self-preferencing or refusing to deal with competitors [S2].

The penalty could reach the greater of 15% of the company's total US revenues from the prior year or 30% of its US revenues in the line of commerce affected by the unlawful conduct—a size designed to outweigh any profit gained from breaking the law [S3].

The new penalties would be on top of, not instead of, existing remedies such as injunctions, private damages, disgorgement, and restitution, so enforcement could both compensate for harm and deter repeat conduct [S3].

DOJ and the FTC would have to issue joint penalty guidelines within a year, considering factors like the volume of commerce affected, the duration and severity of the conduct, and any attempt to conceal it, to make enforcement predictable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant companies—large technology platforms and other firms with monopoly power—that engage in exclusionary or monopolistic conduct would face potentially multi-billion-dollar fines. Their shareholders would absorb those costs and, in theory, the companies would face pressure to stop profiting from market power.

drawbacks.text: Revenue-based penalties of this size attach to conduct that can be legally ambiguous: monopolization cases often turn on contested questions about what counts as exclusionary conduct, and defendants argued the 15%-of-revenue scale could punish aggressive-but-lawful competition and chill legitimate business decisions.

The bill's effectiveness depended entirely on DOJ and the FTC choosing to sue; enforcement agencies under any administration could decline to bring these claims, and the bill gave them sole discretion over which cases to pursue [S2].

Supporters of existing antitrust law argued current remedies—court orders to stop the conduct, private treble damages, and equity relief—already address monopolization, and Congress's own findings acknowledged the bill was layered on top of them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: when the only consequence of illegally maintaining a monopoly is a court order to stop, breaking the law can still be profitable, and a penalty tied to revenue changes that calculation. The main legitimate concern is that monopoly conduct is often legally contested, so penalties that large create a real risk of punishing aggressive competition that later turns out to be lawful; the joint guidelines were an attempt to manage that, but much would have rested on agency discretion. On balance, the bill offered consumers and small businesses meaningful new leverage against dominant firms, with the cost falling on the companies and shareholders profiting from the conduct.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never took it up: after introduction it was sent to the Judiciary Committee, which held no markup or hearing on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar, joined by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, introduced the bill on July 23, 2019 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, whose action list for the bill contains no further activity—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
It drew three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, and it never advanced past the committee before the Congress expired [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with monopoly power that would have faced the new penalties are better off: their conduct remained subject only to the existing remedies the bill's findings called insufficient to deter exclusionary behavior.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant companies that escaped new penalties

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give DOJ and FTC civil penalty authority over monopolization, then saw it referred to Judiciary with no further action.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined Klobuchar in introducing the bill.

for.name: 3 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter on the record—the sponsor, the co-introducer, and all three cosponsors—was a Democrat, with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Dominant firms with monopoly power (large technology platforms and other market leaders)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to fines up to 15% of total US revenue or 30% of revenue in the affected market for monopolistic conduct like self-preferencing or refusing to deal. Its death left their exclusionary conduct subject only to remedies Congress itself found insufficient to deter.

The bill would have handed both agencies a new monetary penalty tool and required joint guidelines for sizing penalties, strengthening their ability to deter illegal monopoly conduct. Without enactment, their toolkit stayed as it was.
